2.text: divided the spoil. The young buck was given to the nephew. The son took

3.text: the team, and the father the remainder. The neighbors said, “It is enough

4.text: for him, because he lost something dear to his heart, the driving-reindeer.”

5.text: I have this description from one of the participants.

6.text: Another case ended more peacefully. In the summer-time another group

7.text: of reindeer had strayed from their own herd and gone to that of a neighbor.

8.text: The herdsmen saw that one of the animals was quite fat, and wanted to

9.text: slaughter it for their own private use. They threw a lasso; but it snapped

10.text: in two, and the reindeer escaped with a fragment of the lasso wound around

11.text: its antlers. Two hours later the master of the first camp came to the other

12.text: herd, bringing with him the fragment of thong. The reindeer came back to

13.text: him, and he rightly guessed who were the authors of this attempt to steal.

14.text: “Whose lasso is this?” asked he, laughing. He was an old man, and no

15.text: further trouble arose from the incident. Moreover, the herds were too near

16.text: to each other. Under such conditions, the reindeer frequently become inter-

17.text: mingled, and the herdsmen consider it no great crime to slaughter a strange

18.text: reindeer when it comes to their herd. Sometimes they will even slaughter a

19.text: reindeer, and then, of their own free will, confess to the owner, “Oh, I stole

20.text: your reindeer.” Then, of course, they give him a good reindeer from their

21.text: own herd. I mentioned before that on the Arctic seashore, in the summer-

22.text: time, the mutual stealing of reindeer comes to be a serious annoyance.

23.text: One of my acquaintances, Leuˊtɪqai by name, said to me concerning the

24.text: matter, “It is too bad for one to stay in summer on the Palauˊ River. The

25.text: herdsmen steal too much. When I was staying there, in almost every hollow

26.text: I found the carcasses of my reindeer. The legs were cut off and consumed,

27.text: and everyhting else was left to rot;¹ and whomsoever you asked, ‘Who left

28.text: that carcass here?’ the answer was always, ‘I do not know.’ One time I caught

29.text: Qoptɪˊɪrg̣ɪn, son of Tɪˊqo, sitting by a slaughtered reindeer, gnawing at a

30.text: thigh-bone. I asked him, ‘Why did you not carry the carcass to your father,

31.text: who is also hungry, since you slaughtered it?’ He said nothing. ‘Or perhaps,

32.text: if you desire it, I shall give you my whole herd.’ We both took off our

33.text: fur shirts. He was a young man, but could not do anything, because great

34.text: anger overcame me. I threw him down, then seized my thick rawhide girdle,

35.text: and struck him with that upon his bare back until it was all covered with

36.text: blood. After that I resolved never again to go to that land of thieves.”

37.text: Leuˊtɪqäi was a man of about fifty and of mild temper; but the wrong had

38.text: been repeated too often to let it go unpunished.

39.text: “Chief” Eiˊheli and the Maritime trader Čêpaˊt also had a quarrel over

40.text: the stealing of reindeer. Čêpaˊt, being of Maritime origin, had not had any

41.text: ¹ The Chukchee herdsmen, when they have no cooking-kettle and no fuel, but feel keen hunger, some-

42.text: times slaughter a reindeer and feed on its four legs. The hard sinews and the marrow of the bones are eaten

43.text: raw. The rest necessarily has to be left on the spot.
